analysis.one_liner: Makes police use of force against protesters a federal civil rights crime and drops the death penalty as a possible punishment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House on May 29, 2025 with two cosponsors and has sat in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends a federal criminal civil rights law that already makes it a crime for government officials — including police officers — to violate someone's constitutional rights while acting under color of law. It would write into that statute that using force while responding to a protest counts as such a violation, and it would remove the death penalty from the list of possible punishments, even in cases where someone dies. The bill had not received any committee action since being referred.
analysis.who_benefits: People who attend protests — demonstrations, marches, and rallies — would gain a clearer federal criminal remedy when officers injure or kill protesters. Under current law, prosecutors can already charge officials under the same statute, but the bill would remove any argument that protest policing is somehow outside it, and it would make clear that force used against demonstrators falls within the law's reach. It would also spare defendants, including officers, from facing a possible death sentence.

how_it_helps.text: The bill specifies that use of force during a response to a protest constitutes a deprivation of federally protected rights under the criminal civil rights statute (18 U.S.C. § 242), closing off any argument that protest policing falls outside the law.
It removes the death penalty as a sentencing option when a rights violation results in death or when aggravating factors are present, meaning the harshest possible punishment becomes imprisonment.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and other government officials would face clearer and broader federal criminal exposure for force used during protest responses, in addition to the liability they already carry under the same statute. Federal prosecutors and courts would bear the cost of litigating the new language, including questions about how broadly 'a response to a protest' reaches — for example, whether it covers crowd-control decisions made in chaotic, fast-moving situations. Some victims' families might also see the removal of the death penalty as a lighter punishment for the worst cases.

drawbacks.text: The phrase 'use of force during a response to a protest' is broad, and officers acting in good faith in fast-moving crowd situations could face federal charges over split-second decisions; courts would have to work out where the line falls.

Because the underlying statute already criminalizes officials' deprivation of rights under color of law, the bill's practical effect may be limited to clarifying that protest contexts are covered, rather than creating a genuinely new remedy.

Removing the death penalty lowers the maximum punishment for the most severe cases — a killing by an official during a protest response could no longer be punished capitally — which some see as too lenient even as others welcome it on abolition grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a meaningful clarification for protesters' civil rights, but its added value over the existing statute is modest, since prosecutions under 18 U.S.C. § 242 are already possible and its willfulness requirement is a high bar. The death penalty removal is a genuine policy choice with arguments on both sides — it eliminates capital punishment for official killings during protests but also guarantees that even the worst cases cap out at imprisonment. The broad protest-response language is the most consequential and most contestable part.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and has seen no committee action since, so no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 29, 2025, joined by Rep. Bennie Thompson and Rep. Pramila Jayapal.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action the bill has received.
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further committee or floor action has been recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet from the bill's provisions, but because it has not moved, law enforcement officers face no new federal criminal exposure for protest policing, and protesters have no added federal protection. The outcome so far simply preserves the legal status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement keeps the legal status quo

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 3651 on May 29, 2025 to clarify that force used against protesters is a federal civil rights crime.

for.name: Reps. Bennie Thompson and Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 29, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the months since.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats — Omar, Thompson, and Jayapal — are attached to the bill, and with no committee or floor action yet, no Republican position has been recorded either way.

industries.industry: Law enforcement (police departments and officer unions)
industries.note: The bill widens federal criminal exposure for officers who use force during protest responses, which police unions and departments have historically resisted in accountability legislation. At the same time, it removes the death penalty as a possible sentence, which reduces the worst-case punishment for officers. Its interest runs against the public's demand for accountability, with the death-penalty change as the one mitigating piece.

industries.industry: Federal criminal justice system (prosecutors and courts)
industries.note: Prosecutors would gain explicit statutory cover to charge protest-related force, but courts would have to define how broadly 'a response to a protest' reaches, creating new litigation.

analysis.trajectory: With three total sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee movement in the months since referral, the bill is very likely to die quietly in the House Judiciary Committee, as most privately introduced criminal-law amendments do. It would need the committee chair to schedule a markup and the full House to take it up, neither of which shows any sign of happening in the 119th Congress.
